# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's orbital period matches its rotational period, causing one hemisphere to face its star eternally while the other remains in perpetual darkness. This phenomenon, common among close-orbiting exoplanets, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most dramatic consequence is the stark temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in continuous stellar radiation, can reach scorching temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out entirely. On a tidally locked planet without sufficient atmosphere, this divide would render most of the surface inhospitable.

However, atmospheres and oceans serve as powerful climate equalizers. Winds transport heat from the dayside to the nightside, moderating temperatures across the globe.
